reader_summary: I understand the two routes to taking this model to a smaller computer. Quantization stores an approximation of the same weights with fewer bits; a portable Dense student first has fewer parameters and may then learn from a fixed teacher. In the toy layer the 32 FP32 weights and four biases need 144 bytes; packed 4-bit weights plus four FP32 row scales and four FP32 biases need 48 bytes. This proves a storage reduction for this object, not faster CPU arithmetic, smaller loaded-model RAM, or preserved task behavior. The reported joint PTQ models kept 78/90 whole-question correctness although a 4-bit response changed, and the smaller CE/KD students scored 62/90 and 61/90. The tool example makes the KD failure concrete: it requested 1+9 for a 1+8 question, then even misread the tool result. The distillation mixture and exercise become understandable using the named links. I still need brief explanations or direct prerequisite links for the branch identities and the task categories used to interpret the deployment tables; the current section assumes that context without supplying it.

program_explanation.details: I ran the exact fenced Python in a fresh offline CPU process using existing .venv torch 2.14.1+cpu. Seed 42 fixes the layer initialization; nn.Linear(8,4) maps one row of eight input features to four output features with 32 weights and four biases. QuantizedLinear receives that layer, so the comparison is against a quantized copy of those weights. torch.ones(1,8) supplies the one all-ones input; no_grad means no gradient bookkeeping or training. Subtraction compares corresponding outputs, abs makes signed differences positive, max selects the largest of the four, and item produces a Python number. The first sum counts parameter elements times bytes per element; storage_bytes counts only stored tensors. Actual stdout was 144 bytes and 48 bytes with max difference 0.046346306800842285. All important input, shape, counting and error lines have prose explanations. No source/code/checker changes were made.

exercise.details: Before executing I saved the prediction that changing only bits=4 to bits=8 leaves the 144-byte FP32 layer unchanged, changes 32 packed 4-bit weights from 16 to 32 bytes, and leaves four FP32 scales and four FP32 biases at 16 bytes each: total 64 bytes. I expected finer levels to reduce this particular output difference without claiming a guarantee. The bounded CPU run printed 144 and 64 bytes with maximum difference 0.0037038326263427734. This is a check of one layer and one input, not deployment capability, RAM or speed.

own_explanation.problem: Choose a practical delivery format for a smaller computer while keeping cost and answer-quality comparisons separate. Compressing stored weights and changing to a smaller architecture are different decisions.
own_explanation.formula: The KD objective is 0.5 CE + 0.5 T^2 KL(p_T || q_T). CE uses the standard answer; p_T is the fixed teacher distribution and q_T the student distribution at the same effective temperature T=2. In the linked explanation, a distribution is obtained by softmax(scores/T); a larger T makes secondary candidates more visible while preserving score order. KL sums p_i(log p_i - log q_i) over corresponding candidates, then the helper averages valid answer positions. The forward direction uses teacher probabilities as weights. T^2=4 is applied once within the helper, so the outer mixing coefficient is 0.5, not an extra multiplication by four. Only the student is updated.
own_explanation.relevant_numbers: The main FP32 tensor storage 1,312,512 bytes matches 328,128 parameters times four bytes. The cited joint 4-bit and 8-bit tensor payloads are 248,864 and 402,720 bytes, while their actual experiment-time files are 275,381 and 429,365 bytes. All three scored 78/90, about 86.7%, but 4-bit changed one generated ID sequence; 8-bit showed no sequence difference on those 90 questions. The DPO comparison branch changed two 4-bit sequences at the same score. The two-layer width-48 Dense student has 79,920 parameters, so its FP32 tensor bytes are 319,680. The two student learning recipes start alike, have the same 350 updates and 145,163 effective answer positions, both score 59/84 on validation, then differ 62/90 versus 61/90 on the final check. KD 4-bit tensor bytes drop to 91,680 and the cited file to 106,229, still scoring 61/90 despite six changed outputs/actions. These are the prose-reported results, not models I loaded or trained.
own_explanation.how_to_check: For the exercise, count weight bits separately from scale and bias overhead; keep the same seed, source layer and input; change only bits to 8; compare storage bytes and the maximum difference. To judge a full delivery, reload the saved artifact and assess common held-out questions and individual responses, with file size, tensor storage, speed and peak memory recorded as distinct quantities.
